title: LLM foundations
task_statement: Explain how a model produces output, what limits its input and output, and how a tool call returns control to the app. (Inference: task wording from repo lesson 7-3A, not from the exam guide)

components.name: Context window
components.first_principle: The context window holds every input token and every output token of a turn, so all of them share one budget.
steps: Everything in a request counts toward the context window.
The system prompt, the messages, the tool results, and the tool definitions all count.
Thinking tokens and text output count too.
The max_tokens value caps the output for each response.
An input longer than the window returns a 400 invalid_request_error.
On Claude 4.5 models and newer, output stops with model_context_window_exceeded when generation reaches the limit.
Use the token-count endpoint before a large request.
pros: A 1M-token window fits long documents in one request for listed models.
Earlier tool results stay available to the model in the same turn.
Each response reports its token usage.
cons: Accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows, which the docs call context rot.
Cached prompt prefixes still occupy the window.
Long inputs raise the token count of every turn.
use_when: The task needs many documents or a long conversation in one request.
The expected output fits inside the max_tokens cap.
do_not_use_when: The input alone exceeds the model window. Shorten or split the input first.
A short prompt answers the task. Extra context adds cost and can reduce focus.

constraints.choice: Use the 1M-token window for listed models and the 200k window for older models.
constraints.combination: Use server-side compaction when a conversation nears the window.

constraints.choice: Estimate tokens before a large request.
constraints.combination: Cache stable prefixes to cut the cost of repeated input.

constraints.choice: Set max_tokens to the output size that the task needs.
constraints.combination: Stream the output when the first tokens matter.

constraints.choice: Read stop_reason before you accept a response.
constraints.combination: Treat model_context_window_exceeded as a truncated answer.

components.trap: A bigger window looks like the fix for missed details, but context rot means more tokens can lower recall.
components.decision_rule: Fit the request inside the window with room for max_tokens, then select what enters the window.

components.name: Model tier choice
components.first_principle: Each tier trades speed and price against capability, so the choice follows the quality target and the budget. (Inference)

nodes.label: Tier list with price and speed
Results on a fixed test set

steps: Name the task and the quality target.
List the tiers with their price, speed, and context window.
Run the same evaluation set on two tiers.
Keep the least costly tier that meets the quality target.
Set the model field to the ID for the platform in use.
Test the choice again after each model migration.
pros: Tiers give a clear trade-off between price, speed, and capability.
A tier change keeps the same request shape.
A test set replaces a guess about which model is large enough.
cons: Model IDs differ by platform, so a copied ID can fail.
Prices and retirement dates change over time.
A smaller tier can miss a hard task, and the miss may show no error.
use_when: A high-volume task with a clear output format needs low latency.
A hard reasoning task fails the quality target on a smaller tier.
do_not_use_when: The largest tier is chosen with no quality test. (Inference)
The design uses a model that is near retirement. Plan a migration first.

constraints.choice: Pick the lowest price tier that passes the test set.
constraints.combination: Price the expected volume before the choice is final.

constraints.choice: Use the fastest tier for high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks.
constraints.combination: Raise the effort setting when the quality test fails. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Match the tier to the complexity of the task.
Record each model retirement date in the design record.
constraints.combination: Plan the migration before the retirement date.

components.name: Tool call loop
components.first_principle: The model requests a tool call, and your code runs the operation and returns the result.
steps: Send the tools array and the user message in one request.
Claude returns a tool_use block with a tool name and a JSON object of arguments.
Your code runs the tool.
Claude never receives your implementation of the tool.
Your code sends the output back in a tool_result block.
Repeat while stop_reason is tool_use.
Stop the loop on end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, or refusal.
pros: Your app keeps control of execution and permissions.
The tool schema gives typed inputs to your code.
Server tools run on Anthropic infrastructure with no code on your side.
cons: Each client tool call adds one round trip.
Your code must enforce a stop rule for the loop. (Inference)
Tool results count toward the context window.
use_when: The task needs an action with side effects, such as an update to a record.
The task needs fresh or external data.
do_not_use_when: The model can answer from its training. No tool call is needed.
A single prompt answers the question and no action runs.

constraints.choice: Log each tool_use block and its result.
constraints.combination: Record the request ID of each turn.

constraints.choice: Run parallel tool_use blocks concurrently, and return all results in one user message.
constraints.combination: Use server tools to avoid a client round trip.

constraints.choice: Run side-effect tools in your code behind your permission checks.
Defer large tool sets with the tool search tool.
Cache the stable tool definitions with prompt caching.

components.exam_tie: F2. Expect a scenario where the model must take an action. The credited answer runs the tool in app code and returns a tool_result. (Inference)
components.trap: A design where the model calls the external API directly looks simpler. The model never runs anything on its own, so your app must run the client tool.
components.decision_rule: Run every client tool in your code and return each result in a tool_result block.
components.exam_tip: If stop_reason is tool_use, run the tools before you read the text as the final answer.

decision_flow:
flowchart TD
  A{Input fits window with max_tokens?} -->|No| B[Split or curate input]
  A -->|Yes| C{Model must act or fetch data?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Client tool loop with tool_result]
  C -->|No| E{Quality passes on smaller tier?}
  E -->|Yes| F[Use smaller tier]
  E -->|No| G[Use larger tier or higher effort]
cheatsheet:
flowchart LR
  W[1M window for listed models] --> B[Input plus max_tokens]
  B --> O{Fits?}
  O -->|No| S[Split or curate input]
  O -->|Yes| T[Tier by test set]
  T --> L[tool_use loop]
  L --> R[stop_reason check]
  R --> E[Final answer]

patterns.rule: Run the tool in app code and return a tool_result block.
